text: Every Published article a user reads carries a simple feedback control: Helpful, or Not Helpful. Each response is tracked against the article, building up a real, visible signal — not a guess, not an anecdote from one annoyed caller, but an aggregated rating a Knowledge manager can actually see.

An article with a strong Helpful ratio is doing its job. An article trending toward Not Helpful is telling the Knowledge manager something specific: this content, as written, is not solving the problem it claims to solve. A Knowledge manager implementing this well treats a falling ratio as a trigger to pull that article back into Draft for revision, where it goes back through Review and the approval gate before being Published again.

When an article is genuinely outdated — the process it describes no longer exists, the tool it references has been replaced — the correct move is Retired, a distinct Workflow state, not deletion. Retiring removes it from active search so end users don't stumble onto stale guidance, while deleting the record would destroy its entire history: who wrote it, when it was reviewed, what feedback it accumulated, what it actually said at any point in its life. That history matters for audit and compliance, and for simply answering what the team used to tell people.

A well-implemented Knowledge Base doesn't wait for Not Helpful votes to pile up before anyone looks again. A real cadence — a scheduled job checking each article's last updated date — flags anything that has gone twelve months or more without review, whether or not it's collected negative feedback yet. Content nobody has touched in a year is content nobody has verified is still accurate.

Problem Management's Known Error Database, back in Chapter 2, generates its own articles — published guidance describing a known problem and its workaround, stored as kb_knowledge records like any other. Those articles follow this exact same lifecycle, and should be retired once the underlying problem is permanently fixed and the workaround is no longer needed. A Known Error article that outlives its usefulness and never gets retired is exactly what a twelve-month review cadence is built to catch.

Real feedback, a real distinction between retiring and deleting, and a cadence that catches what feedback alone might miss. Next up: the lab, putting this whole chapter together into one real implementation.
